meta.description: Engineering term glossary for EngCalcs translation prompts. Preferred translations per language to prevent term drift across calculators and sprints.
meta.usage: Inject relevant entries as context in translation prompts: 'Use these preferred translations for technical terms: [terms for this calculator prefix]'. Entries with empty strings need a sprint to fill.
meta.confidence_notes: Translations marked with (?) in comments need native-speaker review. Empty string = not yet translated.

terms.context: Volumetric flow rate. Appears in every calculator. Use the hydraulic/civil engineering term for discharge volume per unit time, not a general word for 'water flowing'.
terms.translation_notes: Spanish has two common terms: 'caudal' (Spain, South America) and 'gasto' (Mexico). Lead with 'caudal'. Portuguese: 'vazão' (Brazil) or 'caudal' (Portugal) — lead with 'vazão'.

terms.context: Flow velocity (speed of water). Appears in all calculators.
terms.translation_notes: Most languages use a direct cognate of 'velocity'. Do not use a word meaning 'speed' in a general sense if a more precise hydraulic term exists.

terms.context: Energy loss expressed as a height of water column. Appears in Darcy-Weisbach, Hazen-Williams, Manning pipe, and Penstock calculators. Distinct from 'pressure drop' — use the hydraulic engineering term.
terms.translation_notes: 'Head' in the hydraulic sense (energy per unit weight) does not translate literally in many languages — use the established civil/hydraulic engineering phrase.

terms.context: Cross-sectional flow area divided by wetted perimeter. Appears in Manning calculators.
terms.translation_notes: Standard term in hydraulic engineering — most languages use a direct translation. Do not confuse with 'pipe radius'.

terms.context: Length of the channel or pipe boundary in contact with flowing water. Appears in Manning calculators.
terms.translation_notes: Use the standard hydraulic engineering phrase. 'Wetted' here means 'in contact with water', not 'soaked'.

terms.context: Manning's n — empirical roughness coefficient used in the Manning formula for open-channel and pipe flow.
terms.translation_notes: Always include 'Manning' as a proper noun. The coefficient itself (n) needs no translation — only the label does. Do not translate as generic 'roughness coefficient' without 'Manning'.

terms.context: Darcy-Weisbach friction factor. Dimensionless coefficient in the Darcy-Weisbach head loss equation. Distinct from Hazen-Williams C coefficient.
terms.translation_notes: Use the hydraulic/civil engineering term. In some languages, 'friction' and 'resistance' terms compete — prefer 'friction' to match the Darcy-Weisbach naming convention.

terms.context: Coefficient correcting theoretical orifice or weir flow for real-world contraction and friction effects. Appears in Orifice and Weir calculators.
terms.translation_notes: The 'discharge' here refers to flow rate, not the verb. Use the hydraulic engineering compound term.

terms.context: A flow-measurement or water-control structure — a barrier across a channel over which water flows. Appears in Weir Flow Simple and Weir Flow Irregular calculators.
terms.translation_notes: In an irrigation context, the term often overlaps with 'diversion dam' or 'check structure'. Use the term most common among irrigation field workers in the target language, not a purely civil-engineering dictionary term.

terms.context: A submerged or free-flowing opening through which water discharges under head. Appears in Orifice Flow and Orifice Drain Time calculators.
terms.translation_notes: In irrigation contexts, often the opening of a headgate or pipe turnout. Use the hydraulic engineering term, not a general word for 'hole' or 'opening'.

terms.context: Angular rock placed to resist erosion on channel beds and banks. Appears in Manning Trapezoidal Channel and Rock Chute calculators.
terms.translation_notes: No direct single-word equivalent in most languages. Use the established local engineering term — this varies significantly by country. In Spanish, 'enrocado' (general) or 'escollera' (bank protection) are both used; lead with 'enrocado'.

terms.context: Ratio of outflow to inflow in a canal reach — measures how much water delivered at the head is received at the tail. Appears in Canal Seepage calculator. E_c = Q_out / Q_in.
terms.translation_notes: This is the most terminology-sensitive term in the suite. 'Conveyance' means transport of water along a canal — do not use a general word for 'efficiency' alone. The term should convey 'how well the canal transports water without loss'.

terms.context: Water lost from a canal through the bed and banks by percolation into the soil. Appears in Canal Seepage calculator.
terms.translation_notes: Use the irrigation/canal engineering term for slow percolation loss, not a word implying leakage through a crack or structural failure.

terms.context: Pressure pipe carrying water from a reservoir or headpond down to a turbine in a micro-hydro system. Appears in Penstock Design and Micro-Hydro Power calculators.
terms.translation_notes: 'Penstock' is a specialized term with no exact one-word equivalent in many languages. Use the established civil/hydro engineering phrase for 'pressure conduit' or 'force main to turbine'.

terms.context: Total elevation difference between the headpond water surface and the turbine — before subtracting penstock losses. Appears in Penstock Design and Micro-Hydro Power calculators.
terms.translation_notes: 'Gross' means total/before-deduction. Pair with 'net head' for clarity. Use the hydro-power standard term.

terms.context: Effective head available at the turbine after subtracting penstock friction and minor losses from gross head. H_net = H_gross - h_L.
terms.translation_notes: 'Net' means after-deduction. Pair with 'gross head'. Use the hydro-power standard term.

terms.context: Overall efficiency of a micro-hydro power plant — product of turbine, generator, and transmission efficiencies. Dimensionless, 0–1. Appears in Penstock Design and Micro-Hydro Power calculators.
terms.translation_notes: 'Plant' here means the power plant/installation, not a living plant. Use the energy/electrical engineering term for overall system efficiency.

terms.context: Ratio of minimum to average emitter flow rate in a drip or sprinkler system. DU = q_min / q_avg. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
terms.translation_notes: Use the irrigation engineering standard term. 'Uniformity' refers to how evenly water is distributed across the field, not physical evenness of the system.

terms.context: Depth of water applied per unit time by a drip or sprinkler system. PR = q / A_e. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
terms.translation_notes: In irrigation, 'application rate' or 'precipitation rate' (for sprinklers) or 'irrigation rate'. Use the field irrigation term. Do not use a water-quality or chemical-application connotation.

terms.context: A drip irrigation emitter (dripper/micro-sprinkler) that delivers water at a controlled low flow rate directly to the soil or plant root zone. Appears in Drip/Sprinkler calculator.
terms.translation_notes: May be called 'dripper', 'micro-emitter', or 'emitter' depending on the language and irrigation tradition. Use the field term most familiar to irrigation practitioners in the target language. Where both drip and sprinkler terms exist, prefer the drip term since the calculator covers both.

terms.context: Water surface elevation on the upstream side of a weir or orifice. Appears in Weir Flow and Orifice calculators.
terms.translation_notes: 'Headwater' is an upstream water surface — do not confuse with 'head' (energy) or 'source' (origin of a stream). Use the hydraulic structure term.

translations.bg: ниво на вода нагоре по течение

terms.context: Water surface elevation on the downstream side of a weir or orifice. Appears in Orifice Flow calculator. When tailwater is above the invert, the orifice is submerged.
terms.translation_notes: Use the hydraulic structure term for downstream water level. Pair consistently with 'headwater elevation'.

translations.bg: ниво на вода надолу по течение

terms.context: Elevation of the bottom (inside bottom) of a pipe, culvert, or opening. Appears in Orifice Flow and Orifice Drain Time calculators.
terms.translation_notes: 'Invert' is a civil/hydraulic engineering term for the lowest interior point of a conduit or opening. Use the established local term — in many languages this is a direct borrowing or a 'pipe bottom elevation' phrase.

terms.context: Dimensionless ratio of vertical drop to horizontal distance (rise/run). Used as channel slope (S_0) and friction slope in Manning and Darcy-Weisbach calculators.
terms.translation_notes: In open-channel hydraulics, 'slope' is the bed gradient — not the angle. Use the civil engineering term for gradient/grade, not a geographic or topographic term.

terms.context: Flow regime in which fluid moves in parallel layers with no lateral mixing. Reynolds number below ~2000. Appears in Darcy-Weisbach calculator flow regime check.
terms.translation_notes: Nearly always a direct cognate or borrowing from the Latin in technical languages. Confirm the local engineering convention.

terms.context: Flow regime with chaotic, irregular mixing. Reynolds number above ~4000. Appears in Darcy-Weisbach calculator flow regime check.
terms.translation_notes: Nearly always a cognate. Some languages distinguish 'turbulent' (adjective) from 'turbulence' (noun) — use the adjective form.

terms.context: Flow regime between laminar and turbulent — Reynolds number roughly 2000–4000. Appears in Darcy-Weisbach calculator flow regime check.
terms.translation_notes: Use the adjective form meaning 'between two states'. Some languages use 'critical flow' for this regime — check local hydraulics convention.
